IQR calculations with mutate(is_outlier…) are used to flag extreme values in loss ratio and profit, and then remove those outlier rows from the dataset.

# Step 1: Compute IQR thresholds for loss_ratio
Q1_lr <- quantile(portfolio$loss_ratio, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
Q3_lr <- quantile(portfolio$loss_ratio, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
IQR_lr <- Q3_lr - Q1_lr

# Step 2: Compute IQR thresholds for profit
Q1_pf <- quantile(portfolio$profit, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
Q3_pf <- quantile(portfolio$profit, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
IQR_pf <- Q3_pf - Q1_pf

# Step 3: Flag outliers for these two columns
portfolio <- portfolio %>%
  mutate(
    is_outlier_loss_ratio = loss_ratio < (Q1_lr - 1.5 * IQR_lr) | loss_ratio > (Q3_lr + 1.5 * IQR_lr),
    is_outlier_profit     = profit < (Q1_pf - 1.5 * IQR_pf) | profit > (Q3_pf + 1.5 * IQR_pf),
    is_outlier            = is_outlier_loss_ratio | is_outlier_profit
  )

# Step 4: Drop rows flagged as outliers
portfolio_drop <- portfolio %>%
  filter(!is_outlier)

text:
4.1 Cost Distribution
This code reshapes the incurred cost data into a long format, computes the empirical cumulative distribution (ECDF) for each claim type, and plots cumulative distribution curves. The purpose is to show how incurred costs accumulate across different claim types, highlighting the spread and scale of claim costs in the portfolio.

The plotThe code















# Reshape incurred cost data into long format
incurred_clean <- portfolio %>%
  select(
    liability_incurred,
    liability_property_incurred,
    liability_injury_incurred,
    property_incurred,
    theft_incurred,
    fire_incurred,
    glass_incurred,
    legal_protection_incurred,
    occupants_incurred
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "claim_type",
    values_to = "cost"
  ) %>%
  filter(is.finite(cost), cost > 0)

# ECDF transformation per claim type
cdf_data <- incurred_clean %>%
  group_by(claim_type) %>%
  arrange(cost) %>%
  mutate(
    cum_pct = row_number() / n() * 100
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Plot cumulative distribution
ggplot(cdf_data, aes(x = cum_pct, y = cost, color = claim_type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = scales::comma,
    limits = c(1.0, NA) ) +
  labs(
    title = "Cumulative Distribution of Incurred Costs by Claim Type",
    x = "Cumulative Percentage of Claims (%)",
    y = "Incurred Cost (log scale)",
    color = "Claim Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 30, 10)
  ) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 3, ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE))











NoteInsight:



The plot reveals that certain claim types, such as liability injury and fire claims, have much higher incurred costs at the upper end of the distribution compared to others. This indicates that while most claims are relatively small, a small proportion of catastrophic claims drive portfolio volatility and can heavily impact profitability.

4.4 Profitability Metrics
loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium
→ Shows what fraction of premium income is consumed by claims. A ratio > 1 means claims exceed premiums (unprofitable).
profit = total_premium - total_incurred
→ The net financial result per policy. Positive = profitable, negative = loss.
This code categorizes policies into bins based on their loss ratio and profit values, then uses bar charts to visualize the distribution of policies across these categories. The purpose is to quickly assess how many policies are profitable, unprofitable, or break even, and to identify the proportion of policies with high or low loss ratios.

The plotThe code















portfolio_bin <- portfolio %>%
  filter(has_premium) %>%
  mutate(
    # Loss ratio bins
    loss_ratio_bin = case_when(
      loss_ratio == 0 ~ "=0",
      loss_ratio > 0 & loss_ratio <= 1 ~ "0-1",
      loss_ratio > 1 ~ ">1",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    # Profit bins
    profit_bin = case_when(
      profit < 0 ~ "Negative",
      profit >= 0 & profit < 250 ~ "0-250",
      profit >= 250 & profit < 500 ~ "250-500",
      profit >= 500 ~ ">500",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

p1 <- ggplot(portfolio_bin, aes(x = loss_ratio_bin, fill = loss_ratio_bin)) +
  geom_bar(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = ..count..), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Loss Ratio Bins", x = "Loss Ratio Category", y = "Count") +
  scale_x_discrete(drop = TRUE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p2 <- ggplot(portfolio_bin, aes(x = profit_bin, fill = profit_bin)) +
  geom_bar(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = ..count..), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Profit Bins", x = "Profit Category", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p1 + p2











NoteInsight:



The charts show that a large majority of policies have a loss ratio of zero, meaning no claims were made, while a smaller but significant group has loss ratios greater than one, indicating unprofitable policies where claims exceeded premiums. On the profit side, most policies fall into moderate profit ranges (0–250 and 250–500), but there is also a notable share of highly profitable policies (>500). This highlights that while many policies generate steady profits, a subset of high‑loss policies erodes overall portfolio performance.

5.2.3 Profit vs Claim Severity
This code bins claim severity into ranges, calculates median profit for each bin, and visualizes the relationship using boxplots with annotated medians.   mutate(

      claim_severity < 1000 ~ "<1k",
      claim_severity >= 1000 & claim_severity < 5000 ~ "1k-5k",

  filter(!is.na(severity_bin)) %>%

  summarise(median_profit = median(profit, na.rm = TRUE))

       aes(x = severity_bin, y = profit, fill = severity_bin)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-400000 , 200000 )) +
  geom_text(data = summary_stats,
            aes(x = severity_bin, y = median_profit,
                label = scales::comma(round(median_profit, 0))),
            vjust = -0.5, fontface = "bold", color = "darkred") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Profit vs Claim Severity",
    x = "Claim Severity Bin",
    y = "Profit"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +

    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )











NoteInsight:



Policies with low claim severity (<1k) generally remain profitable, with median profit close to zero but positive.
As claim severity increases (1k–5k and 5k–20k), median profits turn negative, showing that moderate claims already erode profitability.
The highest severity bin (>20k) has the largest negative median profit (≈ –70k) and widest spread, confirming catastrophic claims are the biggest threat to portfolio stability.
Overall, profitability declines sharply as claim severity rises, emphasizing the importance of managing high‑cost claims to protect portfolio performance.
